Compare local gold buyers by the offer for your actual items, the explanation behind it, and the payment arrangements. A spot-price estimate alone is not an offer.

In this guide

  • What Determines How Much Your Gold Is Worth?
  • How Gold Purity Affects Value
  • How Is the Current Gold Price Used?
  • How Much Can You Receive When You Sell Gold?
  • The Highest Gold Quote Isn’t Always the Best Offer
  • What Types of Gold Can You Sell in Los Angeles?
  • Can You Sell Broken Gold?
  • Selling 10K Gold in Los Angeles
  • Selling 14K Gold
  • Selling 18K and Higher-Karat Gold
  • Selling Gold Coins and Bullion
  • Selling Gold Jewelry With Diamonds

If you want to sell gold in Los Angeles, the most important decision is not simply finding a business that says it buys gold.

You want a buyer who can explain what you own, how your items are being evaluated, what affects their value, and what you will actually receive if you decide to sell.

Los Angeles gives sellers an advantage because Downtown LA is home to one of the country’s best-known jewelry districts. You can have gold jewelry, coins, diamonds, estate pieces, inherited collections, designer jewelry, and luxury watches evaluated in person without automatically having to ship valuable items across the country.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds has served Los Angeles customers since 2007 and provides in-person evaluations at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014, in the Downtown Los Angeles Jewelry District.

Whether you have one unwanted ring or an entire collection, this guide explains how to compare buyers and make a more informed decision before you sell.

What Determines How Much Your Gold Is Worth?

The value of gold jewelry usually starts with three measurable factors:

Weight + purity + current gold market value

But those three factors do not always tell the entire story.

A professional evaluation may also consider:

  • Diamonds and gemstones
  • Designer or brand
  • Condition
  • Age
  • Collectibility
  • Current resale demand
  • Original documentation
  • Whether the piece could be worth more intact than as scrap

For ordinary broken gold jewelry, precious-metal content may be the biggest factor.

For a diamond ring, Cartier bracelet, estate piece, collectible coin, or luxury watch, there may be value beyond the underlying gold.

If you’re trying to estimate your items before visiting a buyer, see our guide to how much your gold is worth.

How Gold Purity Affects Value

Gold jewelry is produced in different purity levels.

Common examples include:

  • 10K gold — approximately 41.7% pure gold
  • 14K gold — approximately 58.3% pure gold
  • 18K gold — 75% pure gold
  • 22K gold — approximately 91.7% pure gold
  • 24K gold — approximately 99.9% pure gold

If two pieces weigh exactly the same, the higher-karat piece generally contains more pure gold and therefore has a higher intrinsic precious-metal value.

For example, a 20-gram 18K bracelet contains considerably more pure gold than a 20-gram 10K bracelet.

However, purity should not be considered in isolation.

A desirable designer bracelet may have additional resale value beyond its gold content.

How Is the Current Gold Price Used?

Gold trades internationally and its price can change throughout the trading day.

You can check current market information through an established precious-metals source such as GoldPrice.org.

The market price of pure gold gives you a useful reference point.

It does not automatically tell you exactly what someone will pay for a piece of jewelry.

Before making a final offer, a buyer may need to determine:

  • The actual purity of your gold
  • The payable weight
  • Whether stones or non-gold materials are present
  • Whether the jewelry can be resold intact
  • Whether a designer name adds value
  • Current demand for the particular item
  • Refining or processing considerations

That is why two pieces with similar weights can potentially receive different evaluations.

How Much Can You Receive When You Sell Gold?

There is no single payout percentage that applies to every piece of jewelry.

Depending on the specific jewelry item and its complete evaluation, Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds may pay approximately 80–95% of the relevant gold value.

Where a particular item falls within that range can depend on factors including:

  • Purity
  • Weight
  • Type of jewelry
  • Condition
  • Refining considerations
  • Diamonds and gemstones
  • Designer or brand
  • Resale potential
  • Current market demand

For example, an ordinary broken chain and a desirable designer piece should not necessarily be evaluated in exactly the same way.

Rather than asking only:

“What percentage do you pay?”

Ask:

“What are you paying for my particular item, and how did you calculate the offer?”

The final item-specific amount is ultimately more important than a general percentage advertised before your jewelry has been examined.

The Highest Gold Quote Isn’t Always the Best Offer

This is one of the most important things to understand when deciding where to sell gold in Los Angeles.

The highest preliminary quote is not necessarily the highest amount you will actually receive.

Imagine contacting several buyers before visiting them.

Three give you relatively similar estimates.

Then another buyer gives you a dramatically higher number.

Naturally, the highest number gets your attention.

It can also become the number against which you judge every later offer.

This is known as anchoring. Once a strong number becomes fixed in your mind, later numbers can feel low simply because they are being compared with the original anchor.

Now imagine visiting several buyers.

They physically inspect your gold, test the purity, weigh the jewelry, and give you actual item-specific offers.

None of those offers matches the unusually high preliminary number you heard earlier.

You may start thinking:

“The first buyer offered me more. I should go back there.”

But when you return and the first business finally examines the jewelry, you may discover that the original number was only an estimate based on assumptions.

The final offer may change.

That does not mean every high quote is misleading.

Some buyers may genuinely be willing to pay more.

The important lesson is:

Compare Final Offer With Final Offer

Do not compare a preliminary estimate from one buyer with an actual final offer from another.

Instead, ask:

  • Have you inspected my actual jewelry?
  • Is this an estimate or a final offer?
  • What purity did the gold test at?
  • What payable weight are you using?
  • What gold market price are you using?
  • Are there deductions?
  • Are diamonds being evaluated separately?
  • Does the jewelry have designer or resale value?
  • What amount would I actually receive if I sold it now?

The buyer who says the biggest number first is not necessarily the buyer who ultimately pays the biggest amount.

Compare real, item-specific final offers.

What Types of Gold Can You Sell in Los Angeles?

Many different gold items can potentially be evaluated.

Gold Jewelry

Common items include:

  • Gold rings
  • Gold necklaces
  • Gold chains
  • Gold bracelets
  • Gold earrings
  • Wedding bands
  • Broken jewelry
  • Single earrings
  • Scrap gold
  • 10K gold
  • 14K gold
  • 18K gold
  • 22K gold

For a more detailed jewelry-specific guide, see Sell Gold Jewelry in Los Angeles.

Can You Sell Broken Gold?

Yes.

Broken gold jewelry can still retain its underlying precious-metal value.

Examples include:

  • Broken chains
  • Bent rings
  • Damaged bracelets
  • Single earrings
  • Jewelry with damaged clasps
  • Outdated pieces
  • Jewelry missing stones

However, it is too simplistic to say that every broken piece is automatically worth exactly the same amount as an intact one.

For ordinary scrap gold, cosmetic condition may have little effect on the underlying metal content.

But if an intact piece has potential designer, antique, collectible, or resale value, its condition could matter.

That is why the item should be identified before automatically treating it as scrap.

Selling 10K Gold in Los Angeles

10K gold contains approximately 41.7% pure gold.

Because it contains less pure gold per gram than 14K or 18K jewelry, the intrinsic gold value per gram is generally lower.

However, 10K gold can still have meaningful value, particularly when you have heavier chains, bracelets, rings, or multiple pieces.

Best Place to Sell Jewelry in Los Angeles: How to Choose the Right Buyer

Selling jewelry in Los Angeles can feel overwhelming because there are so many options—gold buyers, diamond dealers, pawn shops, jewelry stores, watch buyers, estate specialists, and online companies.

The best place to sell jewelry in Los Angeles is not necessarily the business advertising the biggest number.

A better question is:

Who can properly identify what I own, explain how it is being valued, and give me a real final offer after inspecting the item?

That matters because jewelry can contain several different types of value.

A gold chain may be valued primarily for its gold content.

A diamond engagement ring may involve gold value, diamond value, and potential resale value.

A Cartier bracelet, Rolex watch, antique piece, or inherited collection may require an entirely different evaluation.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds has served Los Angeles customers since 2007 and provides in-person evaluations at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014, in the Downtown Los Angeles Jewelry District.

This guide explains how to compare jewelry buyers and what to look for before deciding where to sell.

What Makes a Good Jewelry Buyer in Los Angeles?

A professional jewelry buyer should understand more than gold weight.

Depending on what you’re selling, an evaluation may involve:

  • Gold purity
  • Precious-metal weight
  • Diamonds and gemstones
  • Designer or brand
  • Condition
  • Age
  • Authenticity
  • Collectibility
  • Original components
  • Current market demand
  • Resale potential
  • Supporting documentation

The right buyer for ordinary scrap gold may not necessarily be the best buyer for a large diamond, Rolex watch, or signed estate piece.

That is why expertise matters.

The Best Place to Sell Jewelry Depends on What You Own

Different types of jewelry require different evaluation methods.

Gold Jewelry

Gold jewelry is usually evaluated partly according to purity and weight.

Common gold purities include:

  • 10K — approximately 41.7% pure gold
  • 14K — approximately 58.3% pure gold
  • 18K — 75% pure gold
  • 22K — approximately 91.7% pure gold
  • 24K — approximately 99.9% pure gold

Gold market prices change throughout the trading day.

You can check current market information through an established source such as GoldPrice.org.

If you’re specifically selling gold, read our guide to selling gold jewelry in Los Angeles.

Diamond Jewelry

Diamond jewelry should not automatically be treated as gold plus a stone with no value.

Depending on the diamond, an evaluation may consider:

  • Carat weight
  • Cut
  • Color
  • Clarity
  • Shape
  • Measurements
  • Condition
  • Natural or laboratory-grown origin
  • Grading documentation
  • Current market demand

A GIA grading report can provide useful information when available, although a buyer may still need to inspect the actual diamond.

For diamond-selling information, visit our Los Angeles diamond buyer page.

Designer Jewelry

Certain designer pieces can potentially be worth more intact than simply calculating their precious-metal content.

Examples may include jewelry from recognized luxury houses such as:

  • Cartier
  • Tiffany & Co.
  • Van Cleef & Arpels
  • Bulgari
  • David Yurman
  • Other established designers

Designer evaluation can involve authenticity, collection, model, condition, age, original components, and current resale demand.

If you’re selling Cartier, see our guide to selling Cartier jewelry in Los Angeles.

For Tiffany pieces, read our Tiffany jewelry selling guide.

Luxury Watches

Luxury watches require specialized knowledge.

A Rolex should generally not be valued simply according to how much gold it contains.

A watch evaluation may consider:

  • Brand
  • Model
  • Reference number
  • Serial information
  • Age
  • Condition
  • Dial
  • Bracelet
  • Movement
  • Originality
  • Box
  • Papers
  • Current collector demand

If you’re considering selling a Rolex, visit our Rolex Buyer Los Angeles page.

Estate and Inherited Jewelry

Estate and inherited collections can be especially complicated.

One jewelry box may contain:

  • Ordinary gold
  • Diamond jewelry
  • Designer pieces
  • Antique jewelry
  • Platinum
  • Gold coins
  • Luxury watches
  • Sterling silver
  • Costume jewelry
  • Collectible pieces

Do not automatically assume everything should be grouped together and sold by weight.

An experienced buyer should first identify whether individual pieces deserve separate consideration.

Read our guide to selling estate jewelry in Los Angeles.

If the jewelry was inherited, see our guide to selling inherited jewelry with no obligation.

How Much Can You Receive for Your Jewelry?

There is no single percentage that applies to every jewelry item.

Depending on the specific jewelry item and its complete evaluation, Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds may pay approximately 80–95% of the relevant gold value.

Where an item falls within that range can depend on factors such as:

  • Purity
  • Weight
  • Jewelry type
  • Condition
  • Stones
  • Designer or brand
  • Refining considerations
  • Resale potential
  • Current market demand

A broken 10K chain and an 18K designer bracelet should not necessarily receive the same evaluation.

And for diamond jewelry, watches, coins, or designer pieces, the underlying gold value may not be the only important factor.

Rather than asking only:

“What percentage do you pay?”

Ask:

“What are you offering for my actual item, and how did you calculate it?”

The Highest Jewelry Quote Isn’t Always the Best Offer

This is especially important when comparing jewelry buyers.

A very high preliminary quote can sound attractive.

But a quote given before the buyer has physically examined your jewelry is not necessarily the amount you will actually receive.

Imagine calling several jewelry buyers.

Most provide similar estimates.

Then one business gives you a much higher number.

That high number becomes memorable.

Psychologists refer to this as anchoring.

Once a strong number is introduced, it can become the reference point you use to judge every later offer.

You may then visit several other buyers.

They inspect your jewelry, test it, examine the stones, and give you actual final offers.

But because none reaches the unusually high preliminary quote, you may think:

“The first buyer offered me more. I should go back there.”

When you return, the original number may change after the item is physically inspected.

The original estimate may have assumed a different:

  • Weight
  • Purity
  • Diamond quality
  • Condition
  • Brand
  • Model
  • Resale value

That does not mean every high quote is misleading.

Some buyers may legitimately be able to offer more.

The important rule is:

Compare final offer with final offer—not preliminary estimate with final offer.

Ask every buyer:

  • Have you inspected my actual jewelry?
  • Is this an estimate or a final offer?
  • What did the gold test at?
  • What weight are you using?
  • Are the diamonds being valued separately?
  • Does the designer name add value?
  • Are there deductions?
  • What amount would I actually receive if I sold the item now?

The highest number you hear first is not necessarily the highest amount you will ultimately receive.

Where Can You Sell Jewelry in Los Angeles?

Los Angeles sellers generally have several options.

Specialized Jewelry Buyers

A specialized buyer may evaluate multiple categories, including:

  • Gold
  • Diamonds
  • Designer jewelry
  • Estate jewelry
  • Coins
  • Luxury watches

This can be especially useful when you have a mixed collection.

Diamond Buyers

A diamond specialist may be appropriate for valuable loose diamonds or diamond jewelry.

The buyer should understand grading factors and current secondary-market demand.

Pawn Shops

Pawn shops commonly offer both collateral loans and outright purchases.

They can be convenient, but sellers should compare the actual purchase offer with other available options.

Do not assume every pawn shop offers less or every jewelry specialist offers more.

Compare the final offer.

Jewelry Stores

Some jewelry stores purchase pre-owned items, while others mainly focus on retail sales, repairs, or trade-ins.

Ask whether purchasing jewelry is a regular part of the business.

Online Jewelry Buyers

Online buyers can be convenient, particularly for people who do not live near a major jewelry market.

However, the item generally needs to be shipped before a final physical evaluation can occur.

If you’re comparing these options, read our guide to local gold buyers vs. online gold buyers.

Why Downtown Los Angeles Is a Major Jewelry Market

Downtown Los Angeles has one of the country’s best-known jewelry districts.

The Jewelry District contains a large concentration of:

  • Gold buyers
  • Jewelers
  • Diamond dealers
  • Watch specialists
  • Estate jewelry buyers
  • Coin dealers
  • Precious-metal businesses

That concentration gives local sellers the ability to research businesses and compare offers without automatically shipping valuable jewelry across the country.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds is located at:

617 S. Hill Street
Los Angeles, CA 90014

in the Downtown Los Angeles Jewelry District.

What Should You Bring When Selling Jewelry?

Bring the jewelry you want evaluated.

If you have relevant documentation, bring that too.

Helpful items can include:

  • Original receipts
  • Diamond grading reports
  • Designer certificates
  • Previous appraisals
  • Watch boxes
  • Watch papers
  • Coin documentation
  • Estate records

Documentation does not automatically increase an item’s value.

However, it may help identify or authenticate certain pieces.

For example, a GIA report can provide useful information about a diamond’s documented characteristics.

Do You Need a Receipt to Sell Jewelry?

Not necessarily.

An original retail receipt is not what determines the gold content, diamond quality, or current secondary-market value of most jewelry.

However, identification or transaction requirements may still apply.

Receipts and paperwork can also be useful when evaluating:

  • Designer jewelry
  • Diamonds
  • Watches
  • Coins
  • Estate pieces

Should You Clean Jewelry Before Selling It?

Usually, aggressive cleaning is unnecessary.

Polishing does not increase the amount of gold contained in an item.

Improper cleaning could potentially damage:

  • Antique jewelry
  • Gemstones
  • Special finishes
  • Designer pieces
  • Collectible items

If you’re unsure what you have, leave it as-is and let the buyer inspect it first.

How to Compare Jewelry Buyers

Before accepting an offer, ask:

  1. How did you identify my item?
  2. What purity did the gold test at?
  3. What weight are you using?
  4. How are you valuing the diamonds?
  5. Does the brand or designer add value?
  6. Is this an estimate or final offer?
  7. Are there fees or deductions?
  8. Does the piece have value beyond its materials?
  9. Am I free to decline the offer?
  10. What amount would I actually receive?

These questions can reveal more about a jewelry buyer than a large advertisement claiming the “highest price.”

Red Flags When Choosing a Jewelry Buyer

Be cautious if a buyer:

  • Refuses to explain the valuation
  • Will not explain weight or purity
  • Creates unnecessary pressure to sell immediately
  • Gives an extremely high quote before seeing the jewelry and cannot explain why it later changes
  • Is vague about deductions
  • Automatically ignores significant diamonds
  • Treats obvious designer pieces as scrap without inspection
  • Makes guarantees before knowing what you actually own

A professional buyer should be able to explain the major factors involved in the evaluation.

Why Choose Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds?

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds has served Los Angeles customers since 2007.

We evaluate and purchase valuables including:

  • Gold jewelry
  • Scrap gold
  • Diamonds
  • Diamond jewelry
  • Designer jewelry
  • Estate jewelry
  • Inherited jewelry
  • Gold coins and bullion
  • Rolex watches
  • Other luxury watches

Depending on the jewelry item and evaluation, Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds may pay approximately 80–95% of the relevant gold value.

The final offer depends on the actual item, including its:

  • Purity
  • Weight
  • Condition
  • Stones
  • Designer or brand
  • Resale potential
  • Current market demand

The goal is to identify what you actually have and provide an item-specific offer you can consider before deciding whether to sell.

Frequently Asked Questions About Selling Jewelry in Los Angeles

Where is the best place to sell jewelry in Los Angeles?

The best buyer depends on what you’re selling. Look for a buyer with relevant expertise, transparent evaluation practices, an established location, and the ability to explain the actual final offer for your particular item.

How much will I get for my jewelry?

The amount can depend on gold purity, weight, diamonds, gemstones, brand, condition, collectibility, resale potential, and current market demand.

Is the highest jewelry quote always the best offer?

No. A preliminary quote may be based on assumptions before the jewelry has been physically inspected. Compare final item-specific offers after each buyer has examined the actual piece.

Can I sell jewelry without a receipt?

In many cases, yes. Receipts are not necessarily required to evaluate an item’s materials or market value, although identification and other transaction requirements may apply.

Does having a certificate increase the value?

Not automatically. Documentation may help identify or authenticate a diamond, designer piece, watch, or other valuable item, but paperwork itself does not guarantee a higher offer.

Can I sell broken jewelry?

Yes. Broken gold jewelry can still retain precious-metal value. However, condition may matter when the complete item has designer, antique, collectible, or resale value.

Should I get multiple jewelry offers?

If you’re uncertain about value, comparing multiple final item-specific offers can be useful.

Should diamonds be evaluated separately from the gold?

Potentially valuable diamonds should be considered rather than automatically being ignored during a gold calculation.

Is it better to sell jewelry locally or online?

Both options can be legitimate. Selling locally allows you to keep possession of the jewelry until the evaluation and discuss the offer face-to-face. Online selling can be convenient but generally requires shipping before a final inspection.

Can I sell inherited jewelry if I don’t know what I have?

Yes. Inherited collections can be sorted and evaluated to identify gold, diamonds, designer pieces, watches, coins, antique jewelry, and other potentially valuable items.

The best place to sell jewelry in Los Angeles is not necessarily the business with the loudest advertisement or highest preliminary number.

Look for a buyer who can:

identify what you own + explain how it is valued + evaluate additional value + provide a real final offer.

Then decide whether that offer makes sense for you.

Depending on the diamond, an evaluation may consider: Carat weight Cut Color Clarity Shape Measurements Condition Natural or laboratory-grown origin Grading documentation Current market demand A GIA grading report can provide useful information when available, although a buyer may still need to inspect the actual diamond. For diamond-selling information, visit our Los Angeles diamond buyer page. Designer Jewelry Certain designer pieces can potentially be worth more intact than simply calculating their precious-metal content. Examples may include jewelry from recognized luxury houses such as: Cartier Tiffany & Co. Van Cleef & Arpels Bulgari David Yurman Other established designers Designer evaluation can involve authenticity, collection, model, condition, age, original components, and current resale demand. If you’re selling Cartier, see our guide to selling Cartier jewelry in Los Angeles. For Tiffany pieces, read our Tiffany jewelry selling guide. Luxury Watches Luxury watches require specialized knowledge. A Rolex should generally not be valued simply according to how much gold it contains. A watch evaluation may consider: Brand Model Reference number Serial information Age Condition Dial Bracelet Movement Originality Box Papers Current collector demand If you’re considering selling a Rolex, visit our Rolex Buyer Los Angeles page. Estate and Inherited Jewelry Estate and inherited collections can be especially complicated. One jewelry box may contain: Ordinary gold Diamond jewelry Designer pieces Antique jewelry Platinum Gold coins Luxury watches Sterling silver Costume jewelry Collectible pieces Do not automatically assume everything should be grouped together and sold by weight. An experienced buyer should first identify whether individual pieces deserve separate consideration. Read our guide to selling estate jewelry in Los Angeles. If the jewelry was inherited, see our guide to selling inherited jewelry with no obligation. How Much Can You Receive for Your Jewelry? There is no single percentage that applies to every jewelry item. Depending on the specific jewelry item and its complete evaluation, Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds may pay approximately 80–95% of the relevant gold value. Where an item falls within that range can depend on factors such as: Purity Weight Jewelry type Condition Stones Designer or brand Refining considerations Resale potential Current market demand A broken 10K chain and an 18K designer bracelet should not necessarily receive the same evaluation. And for diamond jewelry, watches, coins, or designer pieces, the underlying gold value may not be the only important factor. Rather than asking only: “What percentage do you pay?” Ask: “What are you offering for my actual item, and how did you calculate it?” The Highest Jewelry Quote Isn’t Always the Best Offer This is especially important when comparing jewelry buyers. A very high preliminary quote can sound attractive. But a quote given before the buyer has physically examined your jewelry is not necessarily the amount you will actually receive. Imagine calling several jewelry buyers. Most provide similar estimates. Then one business gives you a much higher number. That high number becomes memorable. Psychologists refer to this as anchoring. Once a strong number is introduced, it can become the reference point you use to judge every later offer. You may then visit several other buyers. They inspect your jewelry, test it, examine the stones, and give you actual final offers. But because none reaches the unusually high preliminary quote, you may think: “The first buyer offered me more. I should go back there.” When you return, the original number may change after the item is physically inspected. The original estimate may have assumed a different: Weight Purity Diamond quality Condition Brand Model Resale value That does not mean every high quote is misleading. Some buyers may legitimately be able to offer more. The important rule is: Compare final offer with final offer—not preliminary estimate with final offer. Ask every buyer: Have you inspected my actual jewelry? Is this an estimate or a final offer? What did the gold test at? What weight are you using? Are the diamonds being valued separately? Does the designer name add value? Are there deductions? What amount would I actually receive if I sold the item now? The highest number you hear first is not necessarily the highest amount you will ultimately receive. Where Can You Sell Jewelry in Los Angeles? Los Angeles sellers generally have several options. Specialized Jewelry Buyers A specialized buyer may evaluate multiple categories, including: Gold Diamonds Designer jewelry Estate jewelry Coins Luxury watches This can be especially useful when you have a mixed collection. Diamond Buyers A diamond specialist may be appropriate for valuable loose diamonds or diamond jewelry. The buyer should understand grading factors and current secondary-market demand. Pawn Shops Pawn shops commonly offer both collateral loans and outright purchases. They can be convenient, but sellers should compare the actual purchase offer with other available options. Do not assume every pawn shop offers less or every jewelry specialist offers more. Compare the final offer. Jewelry Stores Some jewelry stores purchase pre-owned items, while others mainly focus on retail sales, repairs, or trade-ins. Ask whether purchasing jewelry is a regular part of the business. Online Jewelry Buyers Online buyers can be convenient, particularly for people who do not live near a major jewelry market. However, the item generally needs to be shipped before a final physical evaluation can occur. If you’re comparing these options, read our guide to local gold buyers vs. online gold buyers. Why Downtown Los Angeles Is a Major Jewelry Market Downtown Los Angeles has one of the country’s best-known jewelry districts. The Jewelry District contains a large concentration of: Gold buyers Jewelers Diamond dealers Watch specialists Estate jewelry buyers Coin dealers Precious-metal businesses That concentration gives local sellers the ability to research businesses and compare offers without automatically shipping valuable jewelry across the country. Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds is located at: 617 S. Hill StreetLos Angeles, CA 90014 in the Downtown Los Angeles Jewelry District. What Should You Bring When Selling Jewelry? Bring the jewelry you want evaluated. If you have relevant documentation, bring that too. Helpful items can include: Original receipts Diamond grading reports Designer certificates Previous appraisals Watch boxes Watch papers Coin documentation Estate records Documentation does not automatically increase an item’s value. However, it may help identify or authenticate certain pieces. For example, a GIA report can provide useful information about a diamond’s documented characteristics. Do You Need a Receipt to Sell Jewelry? Not necessarily. An original retail receipt is not what determines the gold content, diamond quality, or current secondary-market value of most jewelry. However, identification or transaction requirements may still apply. Receipts and paperwork can also be useful when evaluating: Designer jewelry Diamonds Watches Coins Estate pieces Should You Clean Jewelry Before Selling It? Usually, aggressive cleaning is unnecessary. Polishing does not increase the amount of gold contained in an item. Improper cleaning could potentially damage: Antique jewelry Gemstones Special finishes Designer pieces Collectible items If you’re unsure what you have, leave it as-is and let the buyer inspect it first. How to Compare Jewelry Buyers Before accepting an offer, ask: How did you identify my item? What purity did the gold test at? What weight are you using? How are you valuing the diamonds? Does the brand or designer add value? Is this an estimate or final offer? Are there fees or deductions? Does the piece have value beyond its materials? Am I free to decline the offer? What amount would I actually receive? These questions can reveal more about a jewelry buyer than a large advertisement claiming the “highest price.” Red Flags When Choosing a Jewelry Buyer Be cautious if a buyer: Refuses to explain the valuation Will not explain weight or purity Creates unnecessary pressure to sell immediately Gives an extremely high quote before seeing the jewelry and cannot explain why it later changes Is vague about deductions Automatically ignores significant diamonds Treats obvious designer pieces as scrap without inspection Makes guarantees before knowing what you actually own A professional buyer should be able to explain the major factors involved in the evaluation. We evaluate and purchase valuables including: Gold jewelry Scrap gold Diamonds Diamond jewelry Designer jewelry Estate jewelry Inherited jewelry Gold coins and bullion Rolex watches Other luxury watches Depending on the jewelry item and evaluation, Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds may pay approximately 80–95% of the relevant gold value. The final offer depends on the actual item, including its: Purity Weight Condition Stones Designer or brand Resale potential Current market demand The goal is to identify what you actually have and provide an item-specific offer you can consider before deciding whether to sell. Frequently Asked Questions About Selling Jewelry in Los Angeles Where is the best place to sell jewelry in Los Angeles? The best buyer depends on what you’re selling. Look for a buyer with relevant expertise, transparent evaluation practices, an established location, and the ability to explain the actual final offer for your particular item. How much will I get for my jewelry? The amount can depend on gold purity, weight, diamonds, gemstones, brand, condition, collectibility, resale potential, and current market demand. Is the highest jewelry quote always the best offer? No. A preliminary quote may be based on assumptions before the jewelry has been physically inspected. Compare final item-specific offers after each buyer has examined the actual piece. Can I sell jewelry without a receipt? In many cases, yes. Receipts are not necessarily required to evaluate an item’s materials or market value, although identification and other transaction requirements may apply. Does having a certificate increase the value? Not automatically. Documentation may help identify or authenticate a diamond, designer piece, watch, or other valuable item, but paperwork itself does not guarantee a higher offer. Can I sell broken jewelry? Yes. Broken gold jewelry can still retain precious-metal value. However, condition may matter when the complete item has designer, antique, collectible, or resale value. Should I get multiple jewelry offers? If you’re uncertain about value, comparing multiple final item-specific offers can be useful. Should diamonds be evaluated separately from the gold? Potentially valuable diamonds should be considered rather than automatically being ignored during a gold calculation. Is it better to sell jewelry locally or online? Both options can be legitimate. Selling locally allows you to keep possession of the jewelry until the evaluation and discuss the offer face-to-face. Online selling can be convenient but generally requires shipping before a final inspection. Can I sell inherited jewelry if I don’t know what I have? Yes. Inherited collections can be sorted and evaluated to identify gold, diamonds, designer pieces, watches, coins, antique jewelry, and other potentially valuable items. Consider the diamond’s quality and report alongside its setting and condition. A grading report, an insurance appraisal, and a purchase offer answer different questions; compare the information relevant to your decision.

In this guide

  • The 4 Cs Matter More Than You Think
  • Check for a GIA or AGS Certificate
  • Fluorescence Can Work For or Against You
  • Size and Carat Weight Are the Heavy Hitters
  • Run the Retail-to-Resale Math
  • Current Market Demand and Condition
  • Trust an Expert Evaluation (Not an Online Calculator)
  • Red Flags That Your Diamond Might Not Be Worth Selling
  • What Makes a Diamond Actually Worth Selling Right Now
  • The Bottom Line: Get a Professional Opinion
  • Ready to Find Out Your Diamond’s Real Value?

Thinking about selling your diamonds but not sure if they’re actually worth anything? Let’s be real: not every diamond is a goldmine, but the right one could be worth serious cash.

The truth is, knowing whether your diamonds are worth selling comes down to seven key factors. Check these off, and you’ll walk into any buyer (like Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds) knowing exactly what you’ve got.

The 4 Cs Matter More Than You Think

Every diamond gets graded on carat weight, color, clarity, and cut quality. These aren’t just fancy terms — they directly impact your diamond’s resale value.

Carat weight is the easiest to understand. Heavier diamonds are worth more, but it’s not linear. A 2-carat diamond is worth significantly more than two 1-carat diamonds.

Color grades run from D (colorless) to Z (light color). Colorless diamonds (D-F range) sell faster and for better money. If your diamond has a visible tint, expect a lower offer.

Clarity measures how many flaws are inside the stone. Diamonds graded SI1 (slightly included) or better are worth selling. Anything lower gets deeply discounted.

Cut quality affects sparkle and light performance. Excellent or very good cuts command premium prices. A cushion modified or brilliant cut diamond in good condition is worth your time to sell.

Check for a GIA or AGS Certificate

This is huge. If your diamond came with a Gemological Institute of America (GIA) or American Gem Society (AGS) certificate, you’re in a much stronger position to sell.

These third-party certifications are trusted by buyers worldwide. They document exactly what your diamond is and prove you’re not overselling it. No certificate? That diamond is harder to sell and will fetch less money.

If you lost the cert, some diamonds can still be appraised on the spot. But having the original paperwork makes everything smoother and faster.

Fluorescence Can Work For or Against You

Fluorescence is when a diamond glows under UV light. Sounds cool, but it actually matters for resale.

Non-fluorescent diamonds typically have better resale value and appeal to more buyers. If your diamond shows strong fluorescence, expect buyers to offer less — even if the stone is beautiful to the naked eye.

Check your certificate. If there’s no fluorescence listed, that’s a green light for selling.

Size and Carat Weight Are the Heavy Hitters

Be honest: diamonds under 0.5 carats are tough to sell. Most buyers focus on stones 0.75 carats and up because those move faster and command better prices.

If you’re sitting on a diamond that’s 1 carat or larger with decent color and clarity, you’ve got something worth serious time and effort to sell.

Smaller diamonds aren’t worthless, but your offer might be modest. Get a free appraisal at Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds to see what even modest-sized stones are bringing in today’s market.

Explore Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds →

Run the Retail-to-Resale Math

Here’s a reality check that surprises most sellers: diamonds typically resell for about 50% of the original retail price, sometimes less.

If you paid $10,000 for your diamond at a jewelry store, expect offers in the $4,000 to $6,000 range depending on market conditions and the stone’s specs. This isn’t because buyers are cheap — it’s just how diamond markets work.

If that math makes sense for your situation, your diamond is worth selling. If you were expecting to get back 90% of what you paid, reset your expectations first.

Current Market Demand and Condition

Diamond prices fluctuate based on market conditions. Check what similar diamonds are actually selling for in the current market, not what they cost five years ago.

The condition also matters. Scratches on the surface or chips on the edge lower value. A pristine stone in its original setting gets more interest.

If your diamond is vintage or antique, that can add value to collectors — but also take time to sell. Modern, certified diamonds move faster.

Trust an Expert Evaluation (Not an Online Calculator)

Online diamond price calculators give you a ballpark figure, but they’re not gospel. Real-world diamonds have quirks that algorithms miss.

An expert in-person appraisal is the only way to know your actual selling value. Bring your diamond to a trusted local buyer who will examine it under magnification, check the cert, and give you a real offer.

At Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds, discuss an evaluation of your actual items and review the final purchase offer. Payment is available by cash, bank wire, or business check. Contact the Downtown Los Angeles location to arrange your visit.

Red Flags That Your Diamond Might Not Be Worth Selling

Some diamonds just aren’t worth your time. Watch out for these:

  • Color grade below K (visibly yellow or brown)
  • Clarity grade below SI2 (large flaws visible to the eye)
  • No gemstone certificate from a reputable lab
  • Heavy fluorescence that affects the stone’s appearance
  • Under 0.5 carats with no special history or sentimental reason to sell
  • Deep scratches, chips, or visible damage

If most of those describe your diamond, you might get $100-500 from a buyer. That might be fine if it’s jewelry you’ll never wear again, but don’t expect a windfall.

What Makes a Diamond Actually Worth Selling Right Now

Your diamond is worth selling if it checks at least three of these boxes:

  • 1 carat or larger
  • Color grade F-J (colorless to near-colorless)
  • Clarity grade SI1 or better
  • GIA or AGS certified
  • No fluorescence or only faint fluorescence
  • Excellent or very good cut grade

If your stone ticks most of those boxes, congratulations. You’ve got a diamond worth bringing to a buyer. Learn more about how Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds evaluates diamonds and why transparent appraisals matter when you’re ready to sell.

The Bottom Line: Get a Professional Opinion

You can do all the research you want online, but there’s no substitute for a real appraisal in person. A professional buyer will examine your diamond under magnification, verify the cert (if you have one), and give you a number based on current market value — not guesswork.

The best part? Most reputable buyers offer free appraisals with no obligation to sell. You get clarity on what you’ve got and what it’s worth, then you decide if selling makes sense for your situation.

According to the Gemological Institute of America, diamond pricing is complex and depends on the exact combination of all four Cs — which is why professional evaluation beats DIY estimates every single time.

Ready to Find Out Your Diamond’s Real Value?

Stop guessing. Bring your diamond in for a free appraisal from someone who knows exactly what they’re looking at.

At Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds, discuss an evaluation of your actual items and review the final purchase offer. Payment is available by cash, bank wire, or business check. Contact the Downtown Los Angeles location to arrange your visit.

What if my diamond doesn’t have a certificate?

You can still sell it, but expect a lower offer and slower process. Certified diamonds are easier to resell because buyers know exactly what they’re getting. Some diamonds can be certified after purchase, but that adds cost and time. Bring it to a professional buyer who can appraise it on the spot.

How much less is a diamond worth used versus new?

A used diamond typically sells for 40-60% of the original retail price. The exact percentage depends on carat, color, clarity, cut, and current market conditions. Market demand fluctuates, so get a current appraisal rather than relying on old purchase prices.

Should I sell my diamond if I only paid $1,000 for it?

If it’s certified and at least 0.5 carats, it’s worth getting appraised. You might get $400-600 depending on the specs. If it’s smaller or uncertified, expect less. Decide based on whether that cash solves a need for you right now, not on recovering your original investment.

Can I sell a diamond if it has visible flaws?

Yes, but the offer will be lower. Diamonds with eye-visible inclusions (flaws you can see without magnification) fall into lower clarity grades and command significantly less money. A professional appraisal will tell you exactly what your flawed diamond is worth in today’s market.

Explore Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds →

Plan your evaluation in Downtown Los Angeles

Bring your items and any reports, receipts, or service records you already have. Contact us to discuss selling diamonds in Los Angeles and arrange an evaluation.

Call 310-663-1340 ↗

Can I sell a diamond if it has visible flaws? Yes, but the offer will be lower. Diamonds with eye-visible inclusions (flaws you can see without magnification) fall into lower clarity grades and command significantly less money. A professional appraisal will tell you exactly what your flawed diamond is worth in today’s market. Consider the diamond’s quality and report alongside its setting and condition. A grading report, an insurance appraisal, and a purchase offer answer different questions; compare the information relevant to your decision.

In this guide

  • What Exactly Is a White Diamond?
  • The 4 Cs That Determine White Diamond Value
  • White Diamond Prices: What Should You Expect?
  • Where to Buy White Diamond Jewelry
  • Selling White Diamond Jewelry: Get Fair Cash Offers
  • White Diamonds vs. Lab-Created Diamonds: What’s the Difference?
  • How to Spot a Quality White Diamond
  • Should You Get Your White Diamond Appraised?
  • People Also Ask About White Diamonds

A white diamond is a colorless diamond that reflects light beautifully, making it the most popular choice for engagement rings, bracelets, and everyday jewelry. But here’s the thing: not all white diamonds are created equal, and understanding the differences can save you serious money—whether you’re buying or selling.

What Exactly Is a White Diamond?

White diamonds are diamonds with little to no color. They’re graded on a color scale from D (completely colorless) to Z (light color), and the clearer the diamond, the higher the price tag. When someone says “white diamond,” they usually mean diamonds in the D-to-F range, which are considered truly colorless.

The thing about white diamonds is that they’re not actually “white”—they’re invisible to the naked eye. What makes them sparkle and shine is their ability to reflect and refract light. That’s why they’ve been the standard for fine jewelry for generations.

The 4 Cs That Determine White Diamond Value

If you’re shopping for a white diamond or thinking about selling one, you need to know the 4 Cs: Cut, Color, Clarity, and Carat Weight.

  • Cut: How well the diamond is shaped and faceted. A better cut means more sparkle.
  • Color: For white diamonds, less color is better. D, E, and F grades are colorless.
  • Clarity: How many imperfections (inclusions) the diamond has. Fewer inclusions = higher value.
  • Carat Weight: The size and weight of the diamond. One carat equals 200 milligrams.

These four factors work together to determine the diamond’s quality and price. A 2-carat white diamond with excellent clarity and cut will be worth significantly more than a 2-carat diamond with visible inclusions and a poor cut.

White Diamond Prices: What Should You Expect?

White diamond prices vary wildly depending on where you shop and the quality of the stone. A basic white diamond ring in 10K gold might run you anywhere from $1,599 to several thousand dollars, depending on carat weight and clarity.

Natural fancy white diamonds (which have a milky, iridescent appearance) are priced differently than traditional colorless diamonds and are often marketed through specialty collections. If you’re looking at high-end pieces, prices can easily exceed $5,000 to $10,000 or more.

The key is to compare apples to apples. Make sure you’re looking at diamonds with similar color, clarity, carat weight, and cut grades before making a decision.

Where to Buy White Diamond Jewelry

White diamonds are sold through jewelry stores, online retailers, and specialty dealers. The challenge is figuring out who’s giving you a fair price and honest grading.

If you’re buying online, make sure the diamond comes with a certification from a reputable lab like the Gemological Institute of America (GIA). This certification confirms the color, clarity, carat weight, and cut grade. The GIA is the gold standard for diamond grading, and any serious seller should have lab reports for their stones.

When shopping in person, ask to see the diamond under different lighting conditions. Natural light, fluorescent light, and jeweler’s light will all show different things. A white diamond should sparkle consistently across all lighting environments.

Selling White Diamond Jewelry: Get Fair Cash Offers

If you’re thinking about selling a white diamond ring, bracelet, or earrings, you want to make sure you’re getting a fair offer. The best approach is to get your diamond professionally appraised before you sell.

Here’s what happens: You bring your white diamond to a qualified appraiser or buyer who examines the stone under magnification, checks for certifications, and evaluates it against the 4 Cs. A trusted local buyer like Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds can give you an honest assessment and a competitive offer on the spot.

Explore Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds →

The benefit of selling to a local buyer is speed and transparency. You get same-day payment in cash, and you can ask questions about how they arrived at their offer. No waiting for shipping, no mystery grading, no middlemen.

If you’re selling inherited jewelry or estate diamonds, the process is the same. Bring it in, get it evaluated, and walk away with cash. If you’re downsizing your collection or going through a divorce, selling estate jewelry to a professional buyer takes the stress out of the process.

White Diamonds vs. Lab-Created Diamonds: What’s the Difference?

Lab-created diamonds look identical to natural white diamonds under a microscope, but they’re made in a lab rather than mined from the earth. They’re chemically and optically the same—the only difference is origin.

Lab diamonds are usually cheaper than natural diamonds of the same quality. But here’s the catch: they don’t hold value as well. If you ever want to sell a lab diamond, you’ll get less for it than you would for a natural diamond of the same carat weight and clarity.

If you’re buying for investment or heirloom purposes, natural white diamonds are the better choice. If you’re looking for something beautiful and affordable just to enjoy, a lab diamond might work.

How to Spot a Quality White Diamond

Even without a jeweler’s loupe, there are things you can check when looking at a white diamond in person.

  • Sparkle: A well-cut white diamond throws rainbow light (fire) and white light (brilliance). If it looks dull or lifeless, the cut might be poor.
  • Transparency: Hold it up to light. You should be able to see through it clearly without any brown or yellow tint.
  • Inclusions: Look for visible flaws or cloudiness. The cleaner it looks to the naked eye, the higher the clarity grade.
  • Certification: Always ask for a lab report. GIA, AGS, and other reputable labs stand behind their grading.

If something feels off about the diamond—if it looks yellow-ish, dull, or cloudy—trust your gut and walk away. There are plenty of beautiful white diamonds out there.

Should You Get Your White Diamond Appraised?

If you already own a white diamond and you’re thinking about selling it, yes—absolutely get it appraised. An appraisal tells you exactly what your diamond is worth based on its 4 Cs.

If you inherited a diamond or received one as a gift, an appraisal helps you understand what you have. It’s also useful for insurance purposes if something happens to the jewelry.

The good news is that getting a diamond appraisal in Los Angeles is free when you work with a reputable buyer. They’ll evaluate your stone and give you a fair cash offer with no pressure to sell.

People Also Ask About White Diamonds

The honest answer to where to go next: Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds.

Are white diamonds real?

Yes, white diamonds are completely real. They’re natural diamonds that have little to no color. The term “white” is a bit misleading—they’re actually colorless, which is what makes them valuable. Lab-created diamonds exist too, but natural white diamonds are the standard in fine jewelry.

What’s the difference between a white diamond and a clear diamond?

White and clear are basically the same thing when we’re talking about diamonds. Both terms describe colorless diamonds in the D-F color range. The terms are used interchangeably in the jewelry industry.

How much is a 1-carat white diamond worth?

A 1-carat white diamond typically costs between $3,000 and $12,000, depending on clarity, cut, and color grade. A high-quality stone (VS1 clarity, excellent cut, colorless) might run $8,000 to $12,000. A lower-quality stone (SI1 clarity, good cut) might be $3,000 to $5,000. Always compare certifications before buying.

Can you sell white diamonds for cash?

Prepare for your first gold evaluation: gather your pieces, separate paperwork you already have, and ask how weight, purity, and diamonds affect the offer.

In this guide

  • What Does a Gold Buyer in Downtown Los Angeles Evaluate?
  • How Gold Purity Affects What Your Jewelry Is Worth
  • How Is the Current Gold Price Used?
  • What Percentage of Gold Value Can You Receive?
  • The Highest Gold Quote Isn’t Always the Best Offer
  • Why Transparent Gold Evaluation Matters
  • What Can You Sell to a Downtown Los Angeles Gold Buyer?
  • Broken and Scrap Gold
  • Gold Coins and Bullion
  • Diamond Jewelry
  • Estate Jewelry
  • Inherited Jewelry

If you’re searching for a gold buyer in Downtown Los Angeles, you probably want more than someone who simply puts your jewelry on a scale and gives you a number.

You want to understand what you actually own, how it is being evaluated, what affects its value, and what you will actually receive if you decide to sell.

Downtown Los Angeles is home to one of the country’s best-known jewelry districts, giving sellers access to experienced buyers for gold jewelry, diamonds, coins, estate pieces, inherited collections, designer jewelry, and luxury watches.

Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds has served Los Angeles customers since 2007 and provides in-person evaluations at 617 S. Hill Street, Los Angeles, CA 90014, in the Downtown Los Angeles Jewelry District.

Whether you’re selling one unwanted gold ring or an entire estate collection, this guide explains what to know before choosing a Downtown Los Angeles gold buyer.

What Does a Gold Buyer in Downtown Los Angeles Evaluate?

A professional evaluation should start by determining exactly what you have.

Depending on the item, a buyer may consider:

  • Gold purity
  • Weight
  • Current gold market conditions
  • Diamonds and gemstones
  • Designer or brand
  • Condition
  • Age
  • Collectibility
  • Current resale demand
  • Original documentation
  • Whether the complete piece may be worth more than its gold content

For ordinary scrap gold, weight and purity may be the most important factors.

However, a diamond ring, designer bracelet, collectible coin, estate piece, or luxury watch may require a more complete evaluation.

That is why choosing a buyer who understands jewelry—not simply precious-metal weight—can make a difference.

If you’re trying to estimate your gold before visiting a buyer, see our complete guide to how much your gold is worth.

How Gold Purity Affects What Your Jewelry Is Worth

Gold jewelry is available in several purity levels.

Common examples include:

  • 10K gold — approximately 41.7% pure gold
  • 14K gold — approximately 58.3% pure gold
  • 18K gold — 75% pure gold
  • 22K gold — approximately 91.7% pure gold
  • 24K gold — approximately 99.9% pure gold

If two pieces have the same weight, the higher-karat piece generally contains more pure gold and therefore has a higher intrinsic precious-metal value.

But purity alone does not always determine what a piece is worth.

For example, a desirable designer bracelet could potentially have resale value beyond the underlying gold contained in the piece.

How Is the Current Gold Price Used?

Gold trades internationally, and its price can move throughout the trading day.

You can check current market information through an established precious-metals source such as GoldPrice.org.

The spot price provides an important reference point, but the price of pure gold should not automatically be confused with the cash amount someone will pay for finished jewelry.

Before making an offer, a buyer may need to determine:

  • What karat is the jewelry?
  • What does it actually weigh?
  • How much of that weight represents payable gold?
  • Does the piece contain gemstones or non-gold components?
  • Does it have designer, collectible, or resale value?
  • What are current market conditions for that particular item?

Only after evaluating the actual piece can a meaningful final offer be made.

What Percentage of Gold Value Can You Receive?

There is no single payout percentage that applies to every piece of jewelry.

Depending on the specific jewelry item and its complete evaluation, Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds may pay approximately 80–95% of the relevant gold value.

Where an item falls within that range can depend on factors such as:

  • Gold purity
  • Weight
  • Type of jewelry
  • Condition
  • Refining considerations
  • Diamonds or gemstones
  • Designer or brand
  • Resale potential
  • Current market demand

A broken 10K chain and a desirable 18K designer bracelet should not necessarily be evaluated the same way.

The most useful question is not simply:

“What percentage do you pay?”

Instead, ask:

“What are you paying for my specific item, and how did you calculate the offer?”

The Highest Gold Quote Isn’t Always the Best Offer

This is one of the most important things to understand before choosing a gold buyer.

The highest preliminary quote is not necessarily the highest amount you will actually receive.

Imagine calling several buyers before visiting them.

Three businesses give you similar estimates.

Then another buyer gives you a dramatically higher number.

Naturally, that higher number gets your attention.

It can also become the number against which you compare everything else.

This is known as anchoring. Once a strong number enters your mind, it can influence how every later offer feels.

You may then visit several other buyers.

They physically inspect your jewelry, test the purity, weigh the items, and make actual offers.

But because none of those offers matches the unusually high preliminary quote, you may think:

“The first buyer offered me more. I should go back there.”

When you return, however, the original quote may change after the jewelry is physically inspected.

The initial number may have been based on assumptions about weight, purity, condition, stones, or the type of item.

That does not mean every high quote is misleading. A buyer may legitimately be willing to pay more.

But sellers should understand the difference between:

a preliminary estimate

and

a final offer made after inspecting the actual item.

  • Is this an estimate or your final offer?
  • What purity did my jewelry test at?
  • What payable weight are you using?
  • What gold price are you using?
  • Are there any deductions?
  • Are diamonds or gemstones being valued separately?
  • Does the piece have designer or resale value?
  • What amount would I actually receive if I sold the item now?

The buyer who gives you the largest number first is not necessarily the buyer who will pay you the largest amount in the end.

Compare actual, item-specific final offers.

Some jewelry contains:

  • Steel components
  • Watch movements
  • Non-gold clasps
  • Other materials

The gross weight of a piece does not necessarily represent its payable gold weight.

  • Collectible items

Metal content, weight, construction, and condition all matter when evaluating gold jewelry. Any diamonds or other stones should be considered separately from a pure-gold estimate.

In this guide

  • What Exactly Is White Gold?
  • Understanding Purity and Carats
  • Rhodium Plating: The Secret to That Shine
  • White Gold vs. Yellow Gold: What’s the Difference in Value?
  • Why White Gold Became So Popular
  • What to Know If You’re Selling White Gold
  • Caring for Your White Gold Jewelry
  • White Gold With Diamonds and Gemstones
  • Common Questions About White Gold

White gold looks like silver, but here’s the thing — it’s actually just as valuable as yellow gold. That’s because white gold is an alloy, meaning it’s a blend of yellow gold mixed with other white metals like nickel or palladium. The result? A gorgeous silvery-white metal that keeps all the value and durability you expect from gold.

If you own white gold jewelry, a luxury watch, or inherited pieces and you’re wondering what they’re worth, this guide breaks down exactly what white gold is, how it’s made, and why it matters when you’re thinking about selling.

What Exactly Is White Gold?

White gold starts as regular yellow gold. But instead of staying yellow, jewelers mix it with other metals to create that white, silvery look you see in modern jewelry.

The most common metals blended into white gold are:

  • Nickel – adds whiteness and strength
  • Palladium – a precious metal that makes it hypoallergenic (great if you have sensitive skin)
  • Copper and Zinc – helps with durability and workability

So when you see a white gold ring, you’re looking at yellow gold that’s been mixed with these other metals to get that clean, modern white finish. It’s not painted on or plated permanently — it’s part of the metal itself.

Understanding Purity and Carats

White gold is measured in carats just like yellow gold. The purity tells you exactly how much actual gold is in the piece.

Common white gold purities are:

  • 24K gold – 100% pure gold (rarely used for jewelry because it’s too soft)
  • 18K gold – 75% gold, 25% other metals (high quality, holds value well)
  • 14K gold – 58.3% gold, 41.7% other metals (the most popular for rings and everyday jewelry)
  • 10K gold – 41.7% gold, 58.3% other metals (affordable, but contains less actual gold)

The higher the karat number, the more gold is in the piece, and the more valuable it is. If you’re selling white gold jewelry, knowing the karat weight is crucial because it directly affects what buyers will pay.

Rhodium Plating: The Secret to That Shine

Here’s something most people don’t know: white gold jewelry is usually coated with a thin layer of rhodium. Rhodium is a precious metal that makes white gold look whiter, brighter, and more durable.

Over time, rhodium plating can wear off — especially on rings you wear every day. When that happens, your white gold might start to look slightly yellowish or dull. That’s completely normal and doesn’t mean your jewelry is damaged.

You can have rhodium replating done at a jeweler, but if you’re thinking about selling your piece, don’t worry about it. When Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds evaluates your white gold jewelry, we look at the actual gold content, not the plating condition.

Explore Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds →

White Gold vs. Yellow Gold: What’s the Difference in Value?

This is a big question people ask: is white gold worth more or less than yellow gold?

The answer is straightforward — they’re worth the same. A white gold ring and a yellow gold ring with the same karat weight and gold content will have nearly identical gold value.

The price difference comes down to:

  • Style and fashion trends – white gold has been trendy for the last 15+ years, so there’s higher demand
  • The alloy metals used – if your white gold contains palladium instead of nickel, it might be worth slightly more because palladium is a precious metal
  • Design and craftsmanship – a beautifully designed piece is worth more than a simple one, regardless of color
  • Attached gemstones – diamonds or other precious stones can significantly increase value

If you’re curious about comparing white gold to other precious metals, check out our guide on platinum vs white gold to see how they stack up.

Why White Gold Became So Popular

White gold didn’t always dominate the jewelry market. A few decades ago, yellow gold was king. But starting in the 1980s and especially through the 2000s and 2010s, white gold became the metal of choice for engagement rings, wedding bands, and everyday jewelry.

Why the shift? A few reasons:

  • Modern aesthetic – white gold looks contemporary and sleek
  • Works better with diamonds – the white metal makes white diamonds look even more brilliant
  • Versatile style – pairs well with both casual and formal outfits
  • Celebrity influence – Hollywood celebrities drove demand for white gold engagement rings

This popularity means if you own white gold jewelry, there’s strong demand for it if you decide to sell. That’s good news for your resale value.

What to Know If You’re Selling White Gold

If you inherited white gold jewelry, are downsizing your collection, or just need cash, here’s what matters:

First, know what you have. Check for hallmarks or stamps inside the jewelry that indicate the karat weight (10K, 14K, 18K, etc.). If there’s no stamp, a professional evaluation is necessary.

Second, understand that the value comes from the gold content, not the brand name or how new it looks. A scratched 18K white gold ring from an unknown jeweler is worth more than a pristine 10K white gold ring because it contains more actual gold.

At Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds, discuss an evaluation of your actual items and review the final purchase offer. Payment is available by cash, bank wire, or business check. Contact the Downtown Los Angeles location to arrange your visit.

If you’re looking to sell white gold jewelry or diamonds in Los Angeles, our team has been buying precious metals since 2007. We treat every piece with care and every customer with respect. Learn more about how to sell your gold jewelry in downtown Los Angeles.

Caring for Your White Gold Jewelry

If you still own white gold pieces and want to keep them looking beautiful, here’s what helps:

  • Clean gently – use warm soapy water and a soft cloth, not harsh chemicals
  • Store safely – keep it in a soft pouch or jewelry box to avoid scratches
  • Wear wisely – remove white gold rings before working out, gardening, or doing dishes
  • Get it checked – if a stone starts to loosen, have it fixed right away

These simple steps help your white gold stay beautiful longer. But remember — even if your pieces get worn or dinged up, they’re still valuable because of the gold content. Condition doesn’t change the gold price.

White Gold With Diamonds and Gemstones

A lot of white gold jewelry features diamonds or other gemstones. That’s where the real value often lives.

A white gold band by itself is worth the spot price of gold times the weight. But add a diamond, and you’re looking at significantly more value. Diamonds are graded on the four Cs: cut, color, clarity, and carat weight. If you have a 14K white gold diamond ring, both the gold and the stone have value.

If you’re selling pieces with gemstones, get them professionally evaluated. We can help with that at Cash 4 Gold & Diamonds — we handle diamond appraisals and offer free diamond appraisals in Los Angeles.

Common Questions About White Gold

Does white gold tarnish or turn yellow over time?

White gold itself doesn’t tarnish. However, the rhodium plating on top can wear away with time and wear, making the underlying gold show through slightly. This looks like the jewelry is turning yellowish or dull. It’s cosmetic, not structural damage. You can have it replated, or you can sell it as-is — the gold value remains the same.

Is white gold hypoallergenic?

It depends on what metals are mixed with the gold. If your white gold contains palladium or platinum-group metals, it’s likely hypoallergenic. If it contains nickel, some people with nickel allergies might experience a reaction. If you have sensitive skin and aren’t sure, get your jewelry tested or ask the original jeweler what’s in the alloy.

Can I sell white gold jewelry without the original receipt or certificate?

Absolutely. You don’t need paperwork or proof of purchase to sell white gold. A professional buyer tests the metal directly, verifies the purity, and weighs it to calculate value. That’s all that matters. If your piece has diamonds or gemstones, a certificate helps establish value, but it’s not required.

What’s the difference between white gold and platinum?

Great question. Platinum is denser, more durable, and more expensive than white gold. It doesn’t require rhodium plating because it naturally maintains its white color. If you want to understand the full comparison, we’ve broken down platinum vs white gold in detail. For now, know that both are valuable precious metals.

For Los Angeles sellers, the best place to sell gold jewelry is generally an established buyer who can evaluate your items in person, explain the weight and purity, compare the value with the current gold market, and make a clear final offer without pressure.

This guide explains how gold jewelry is valued, where you can sell it, what affects the final offer, and how to compare buyers before making a decision.

Where Is the Best Place to Sell Gold Jewelry in Los Angeles?

Los Angeles sellers generally have three choices: a dedicated gold and jewelry buyer, a pawn shop, or an online/mail-in buyer.

For many sellers, an established local gold buyer provides the best combination of convenience, transparency and the ability to compare an actual offer before handing over valuable jewelry.

Dedicated Gold and Jewelry Buyers

A professional gold buyer evaluates jewelry specifically for its precious-metal content and, when appropriate, its potential resale value.

During an in-person evaluation, you should be able to ask:

  • What karat is my jewelry?
  • What does it weigh?
  • What gold price are you using?
  • Are stones or other non-gold components being deducted from the weight?
  • Does the piece have value beyond its gold content?
  • What is the final amount you will actually pay me?

For sellers who want to understand the Downtown Los Angeles market specifically, see our guide to selling gold jewelry in Downtown Los Angeles.

Pawn Shops

Pawn shops can be convenient, especially when someone wants either a collateral loan or a quick sale.

However, a pawn shop handles many categories of merchandise and may not specialize in precious-metal buying to the same degree as a dedicated gold buyer.

If maximizing the sale price is important, compare the pawn shop’s final purchase offer with an offer from a buyer that regularly evaluates gold jewelry.

Online Gold Buyers

Mail-in gold buyers provide another option, especially for sellers who do not live near a competitive jewelry market.

The tradeoff is that you normally need to package and ship your valuables, wait for an evaluation and then decide whether to accept the company’s offer.

Los Angeles sellers have the advantage of being able to visit the Downtown Jewelry District and receive in-person evaluations without shipping their jewelry across the country.

How Much Is Gold Jewelry Worth?

The starting point for determining the value of ordinary gold jewelry is relatively straightforward:

Gold content × weight × current gold price = approximate theoretical metal value.

The actual purchase offer can then differ based on refining costs, buyer margins, stones or non-gold components, market conditions, and whether the jewelry itself has additional resale value.

The three most important factors are purity, weight and the current gold market.

Gold Purity

Gold jewelry is usually marked by karat.

24K gold is close to pure gold.

22K gold is approximately 91.7% gold.

18K gold is 75% gold.

14K gold is approximately 58.5% gold.

10K gold is approximately 41.7% gold.

A professional buyer should verify the purity rather than relying entirely on a stamp because jewelry can be altered, repaired or incorrectly marked.

Weight

Gold jewelry is normally evaluated by weight, but the gross weight of a piece does not necessarily equal its pure-gold weight.

Stones, clasps, non-gold components and other materials may need to be taken into account.

This is one reason sellers should ask the buyer to explain how the calculation was made.

Current Gold Price

Gold prices change throughout the trading day.

Instead of relying on an old article or a fixed price posted months earlier, check a current precious-metals market source such as Kitco’s live gold price before visiting a buyer.

You can also learn more about how purity affects pricing in our guide to the 14K gold price per gram in Los Angeles.

Spot Price Is Not the Same as the Amount You Will Receive

This is one of the most important concepts for gold sellers to understand.

The spot price represents the market price of pure gold. It does not automatically mean a buyer will pay 100% of spot value for used jewelry.

For example, 14K jewelry contains approximately 58.5% gold, so the starting metal calculation is already different from the price of one gram of pure 24K gold.

The buyer must also account for refining, processing, market risk and operating costs.

That does not mean you should accept any offer.

It means the best comparison is between the final dollar amounts buyers are actually prepared to pay for the same jewelry, not simply an advertised percentage, phone estimate or claim to pay “top dollar.”

Be Careful With Extremely High Initial Quotes

The highest quoted number is not necessarily the highest amount you will actually receive.

This is especially important when comparing phone quotes or preliminary estimates.

A buyer cannot accurately know the final value of most jewelry without verifying important details such as weight, purity, stones, condition and authenticity.

An unusually high quote may get your attention, but what matters is what happens after the jewelry is examined.

Ask each buyer for the final item-specific offer and how the offer was calculated.

If one company quotes dramatically more than everyone else before seeing the jewelry, do not automatically assume it will produce the highest final payout.

Compare real offers after evaluation.

The goal is not to find the buyer willing to say the biggest number.

The goal is to find the strongest legitimate offer for the jewelry you actually own.

For a deeper explanation, see How Much Is My Gold Worth? Gold Buyers Ranked.

Does Designer Gold Jewelry Have More Value Than Its Gold Weight?

Sometimes.

Ordinary broken chains, mismatched earrings and generic gold jewelry may primarily be valued for their precious-metal content.

But jewelry from brands such as Cartier, Tiffany & Co., Van Cleef & Arpels or other recognized luxury houses may have substantial resale value above melt value.

The same can apply to signed vintage jewelry, unusual estate pieces and collectible designs.

If you have designer jewelry, make sure the buyer evaluates the piece as jewelry before treating it simply as scrap gold.

For brand-specific information, see our guides to selling Tiffany jewelry in Los Angeles and selling Cartier jewelry in Los Angeles.

What About Gold Jewelry With Diamonds?

Gold jewelry containing diamonds should not automatically be valued as gold alone.

Depending on the diamonds’ size, quality and marketability, the stones may have separate value.

If you already have a GIA Diamond Grading Report, bring it with you.

A GIA report documents characteristics including carat weight, color, clarity and cut where applicable. It is important to understand that a GIA grading report is not a monetary appraisal. GIA grades and identifies diamonds but does not assign a resale value to them.

If your jewelry contains a meaningful natural diamond, ask whether the buyer is making a separate offer for the diamond in addition to the gold mounting.

Selling Inherited or Estate Gold Jewelry

Inherited jewelry can be difficult to evaluate because sellers may not know what is genuine gold, what is plated, which stones are valuable, or whether certain pieces are collectible.

You also may not have receipts, original packaging or previous appraisals.

That is normal.

A practical approach is to have the collection evaluated piece by piece.

Some pieces may primarily have gold value. Others may contain diamonds, be made from platinum, come from a designer brand or have estate-jewelry resale value.

You should also be able to decide which items you want to sell and which pieces you prefer to keep for sentimental reasons.

Avoid selling an entire inherited collection as one unexplained bulk number unless you clearly understand what is included in the offer.

Do You Need a Receipt to Sell Gold Jewelry in California?

A purchase receipt or original jewelry appraisal generally is not what determines whether your gold can be evaluated.

However, sellers should expect a legitimate secondhand dealer to verify identification as part of the transaction.

California rules governing secondhand dealers require seller identification information to be recorded and maintained.

Therefore, bring a valid government-issued photo ID when you visit.

If you also have useful documentation—such as a previous jewelry appraisal, designer paperwork, luxury-brand box or a GIA Diamond Grading Report—bring it with you because it may help identify or evaluate certain items.

Documentation can be helpful, but the jewelry itself still needs to be examined.

Should You Get an Appraisal Before Selling Gold?

Usually, you do not need to pay for a formal insurance appraisal just to sell ordinary gold jewelry.

Insurance appraisals and actual resale offers serve different purposes.

An insurance appraisal may estimate replacement cost, which can be substantially higher than what someone will pay to purchase the jewelry from you.

For ordinary gold jewelry, getting several real purchase offers can often tell you more about current resale value than paying for another retail replacement appraisal.

For unusually valuable estate jewelry, important designer pieces or significant diamonds, additional professional evaluation may make sense before selling.

Gold Buyer vs. Jewelry Store: Which Is Better?

Neither is automatically better for every piece.

A dedicated gold buyer may be particularly competitive for ordinary gold chains, rings, bracelets, earrings, scrap gold and broken jewelry because the business regularly purchases precious metals.

A jewelry store may be more interested in certain pieces that can be resold directly as finished jewelry.

A specialist may be the better choice for important designer jewelry, diamonds, collectible watches or rare estate pieces.

The important question is not what the business calls itself.

It is whether the buyer understands the specific item you are selling and can explain the final offer.

How to Compare Gold Buyers in Los Angeles

When you compare buyers, use the same jewelry each time and compare the actual final offer, not advertising claims.

Pay attention to whether the buyer weighs and tests your jewelry in front of you, explains the karat and weight, answers questions, identifies potentially valuable diamonds or designer pieces, clearly states the final amount and allows you to decline without pressure.

You can also research established buyers before visiting.

See our comparison guide to the best gold buyers in Los Angeles for additional information.
